A **WARNING** is raised when the projected 15-minute demand reaches **1,125 kW**.

**Why that level:**
- 1,125 kW is **90% of the 1,250 kW contract capacity** [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-04_glossary.md#EM-04 Glossary > Billing and demand terms > Warning line].
- It is set as an early-warning buffer below the contract so the shift supervisor can bring demand back under 1,250 kW before the interval ends and an exceedance (billed at 2× or 3× the contract price) occurs [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Purpose].

A WARNING can also be triggered earlier by the forecast: if the probability of exceeding the contract in the next hour is **20% or more**, that also raises WARNING [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-04_glossary.md#EM-04 Glossary > Billing and demand terms > P(exceed)].

For reference, the next level up, **ALARM**, fires when projected demand exceeds the 1,250 kW contract or P(exceed) reaches 50% or more [source: docs/knowledge/equipment/EQ-08_cooling_tower.md#EQ-08 Cooling Tower and Pumps Manual > Monitoring alarms that apply].

Under the Taipower high-voltage time-of-use tariff, demand above the contract capacity is billed at a **premium (penalty) rate**, applied per 15-minute interval:

- **Up to 10% over the contract** (i.e., demand between 1,250 kW and 1,375 kW): the excess is billed at **2× the period's contract price** [unverified citation removed]
- **Beyond 10% over the contract** (demand above 1,375 kW): the excess is billed at **3× the period's contract price** [unverified citation removed]

For reference, the plant's contract capacity is **1,250 kW** on a regular contract, and the warning line sits at 90% (1,125 kW) [unverified citation removed] [data: get_plant_overview].

Note that this exceedance charge is on top of the regular demand charge (the monthly per-kW capacity charge) and the time-of-use energy charges — it applies specifically to any 15-minute interval whose demand exceeds the 1,250 kW contract limit.

The night-load baseline (compressed-air leak detector) uses:

- **CUSUM allowance (slack) k = 0.5**
- **CUSUM alarm threshold (decision horizon h = 8)** robust sigmas
- It additionally requires the night load (02:00–05:00) to be **more than 3 kW above expectation** before firing.

The rule compares the compressor night load against the median of the last 6 similar nights.

[source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Trigger]

The load forecaster predicts the **change from an anchor** rather than the demand level because of a limitation of the tree-based model (LightGBM).

**The core reason:** tree models cannot predict values above anything they saw in training, and the plant rarely exceeded its contract during the training data. A level model therefore tends *not* to warn about an exceedance — the first version, which used a level target, actually missed the exceedances. Predicting a change lets the model add a heat-driven or start-up-driven increment on top of the current load, so it can still flag a peak even when the absolute level was never seen in training.

**How the anchor is chosen:**
- Short horizons (15 min to 3 h): the anchor is the last completed interval.
- Day-ahead: the anchor is the same time last week.

The model uses one LightGBM quantile model per quantile (P10, P50, P90) per horizon, with two refinements to keep the confidence bands honest: sorting P10 ≤ P50 ≤ P90 per row to fix quantile crossing, and conformal widening so that 80% of the held-out 14 days fall inside the P10–P90 band.

[source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]

## Operators' actions on a hot afternoon with a demand-exceedance forecast

The plant follows **SOP-06 (Heat Wave Pre-cooling)** for prevention and **SOP-03 (Demand Exceedance Response)** if a warning actually fires. The contract limit is **1,250 kW**, and the forecast raises **WARNING at P(exceed) ≥ 20%** and **ALARM at ≥ 50%** for the next hour. [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Forecast-based warnings]

**Before the peak (pre-cooling):**
1. **Pre-cool the building / chill storage early** — move cooling energy to earlier, cheaper hours so less chiller load falls in the afternoon peak. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Purpose]
2. **Hold non-essential start-ups** — defer optional burn-in loading (BI-01, BI-02) and test runs; delay burn-in loading as soon as status moves to WARNING. [unverified citation removed]

**During the peak (if WARNING/ALARM is raised):**
Follow **SOP-03**, shedding in playbook order and stopping once projected demand is back under contract:

| Order | Action | Equipment | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pause EV charging | EV-01 | 100% |
| 2 | Delay next burn-in loading | BI-01, BI-02 | 35% |
| 3 | Raise chilled-water setpoint +1 °C | CH-01, CH-02 | 4% |
| 4 | Lower compressed-air pressure 0.5 bar | AC-01, AC-02, AC-03 | 3.5% |

[source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 2: shed in playbook order]

- **Never shed** the server room, running molders mid-cycle, or reflow ovens with boards inside. [unverified citation removed]
- Monitor projected demand every interval; you may raise the chilled-water setpoint +1 °C (≈4% of present chiller load) if the pre-cooling margin allows. [unverified citation removed]

**After the peak:**
- Restore shed actions in **reverse order** (pressure → setpoint → burn-in loading → EV charging) once demand is stable and below the **1,125 kW** warning line — do not restore all at once. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 5: restore]
- Record the outcome in the shift log: peak 15-minute demand, actions taken, and any intervals above contract. [unverified citation removed]

## 16 June 2025 Start-up Incident

### Peak demand
The peak 15-minute demand was **1,324.4 kW** at **08:15**, which was **6% above** the 1,250 kW contract [data: get_demand]. Demand exceeded the contract for two consecutive intervals:
- 08:00 → 1,307.1 kW (57 kW over) [data: get_demand]
- 08:15 → 1,324.4 kW (74 kW over) [data: get_demand]

Both were in the off-peak period, carrying penalties of up to **NT$5,106** and **NT$6,652** respectively [data: list_detections].

### What caused it
A **simultaneous start** of 10 machines totaling **805 kW rated**, all switched on within a 3-minute window (07:57–08:27) [data: list_detections]. The detector flagged it as high severity: "10 machines (805 kW rated) started within 3 min; stagger the start-up to cut the demand peak" [data: list_detections].

The demand curve shows the jump clearly: it climbed from ~540 kW at 07:45 to 1,307 kW at 08:00 and 1,324 kW at 08:15 as the whole group of line equipment (AC-02, CH-02, IM-01 through IM-04, RF-01/02/03, and WS-01) started at once, then fell back to ~1,239 kW by 08:30 as ovens settled into heat-up [data: get_demand]. This is exactly the "simultaneous start alert" that SOP-01 expects to be absent [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-01_monday_startup.md#SOP-01 Monday Start-up > Checks after start-up].

### What a 15-minute stagger would have achieved
Re-simulating the same morning with machines started 15 minutes apart would have cut the peak to **1,141.5 kW** — a reduction of **182.9 kW**, bringing demand **below the 1,250 kW contract** and avoiding a penalty of up to **NT$6,652 (US$208)** [data: whatif_staggered_start].

**In short:** the 1,324.4 kW peak was caused by 10 machines (805 kW) starting simultaneously at ~08:00; staggering their start by 15 minutes would have dropped the peak to 1,141.5 kW and kept the plant under contract, avoiding the exceedance penalty.

Yes. A compressed-air leak was detected in September 2025.

**Detection date:** The night-load baseline detector flagged the leak on **2025-09-09** (detected_at), for a rise running from **2025-09-03** across compressors AC-01, AC-02 and AC-03. [data: list_detections]

**Size:** The compressor night base load was up to **18.1 kW** above its usual level, about **+18 kW around the clock**, at medium severity. [data: list_detections]

**Inspection procedure (SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak):**
1. **Purpose:** Follows the night-load baseline detection of a rising compressor load; the loss is clearest at night when production demand is low. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Purpose]
2. **Step 2 – Choose the time:** Do the ultrasonic walk-down in a quiet period, ideally at night or on a Sunday, when machine noise is low and the leak is the largest part of the flow. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 2: choose the time for the walk-down]
3. **Step 3 – Ultrasonic walk-down:** Use an ultrasonic leak detector along main headers and branches; start with areas of most pneumatic use (in particular injection molding); check fittings, quick couplers, hoses, filter/regulator units, drain valves and blow-off nozzles; also check the air dryer area and compressor room. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 3: ultrasonic walk-down]
4. **Step 4 – Tag:** Tag each leak with a numbered tag, record location/type/estimated size (small, medium, large), and photograph where practical. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 4: tag]
5. **Step 5 – Repair:** Isolate and depressurize the section, replace the faulty fitting/hose/valve, re-pressurize and recheck with the detector, then remove the tag and record the closure. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 5: repair]

Note: the estimated financial impact is about **NT$652,462 (US$20,389)/year**, and the procedure warns not to hide a leak by starting AC-02 — fix it instead. [data: list_detections]

**Energy used (Fri 12:00 → Mon 12:00, 17–20 Oct 2025)**

RF-02 (Reflow Oven 2) used **1,976.9 kWh** in that window, at an energy cost of about **NT$6,045** (demand charge and power-factor adjustment are separate) [data: get_energy]. That was roughly 7% of the plant's total weekend energy (27,818 kWh).

Per SOP-02, in the SMT Area checklist (MDB-1):

The procedure's purpose is to prevent idle weekend energy, "the largest single source of which is a reflow oven left in standby." [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-02_weekend_shutdown.md#SOP-02 Weekend Shutdown > Purpose]

Verification step: after shutdown, each reflow oven must read **OFF (at or below 3% of rating)** — check that no reflow oven is IDLE or RUNNING, and confirm the plant night base load is ~500 kW (a much higher figure means something was left on). [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-02_weekend_shutdown.md#SOP-02 Weekend Shutdown > Verification]

## What happened to MDB-3's power factor in early November 2025

On **3 November 2025**, the power factor of board **MDB-3** (Injection Molding) suddenly collapsed from ~0.95–0.96 down to a flat ~0.848–0.852 and stayed there. This matches the recorded incident **S8: "Capacitor bank fault lowers power factor"** (2025-11-03 to 2025-11-13) [data: get_plant_overview]. The active power was unchanged, but the capacitor bank dropped out, so reactive power rose and the PF fell.

## Daytime power factor on 5 November (08:00–17:00)

During 08:00–17:00 on 5 November, MDB-3's power factor averaged **0.849**, ranging from 0.845 to 0.852 [data: get_meter_series]. This is well below the normal ~0.95 level seen before the fault.

## What maintenance should check

Per **SOP-05 Power Factor Check**, the usual cause is a capacitor bank out of service — a tripped breaker or a blown fuse [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Purpose]. Specifically:

1. Verify the capacitor bank on MDB-3 is actually out of service (check breaker position and fuses).
2. The capacitor banks normally cancel 55% of each feeder's reactive power; a dropped bank raises reactive power and lowers PF while active power stays the same [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Background].
3. Isolate the bank, replace the failed fuse, contactor or capacitor, then re-energize [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Procedure > Step 3: restore].
4. If the failure repeats, keep the bank out of service and call the electrical contractor for a full inspection [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Procedure > Step 3: restore].

Note: I can only read plant data and documents — I cannot operate equipment, reset breakers, or send messages. The above is for your maintenance team to act on.
